steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP/vision paper that introduces a new Chinese multimodal (text + image) hyperbole detection dataset built from Weibo posts and an empirical study of detection methods on it. Explain what hyperbole is, why images matter for detecting it, and summarize our contributions and main conclusions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What hyperbole is and why detecting it matters
- Prior work is text-only; images also carry hyperbole
- Weibo as a data source
- Contributions and conclusions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Hyperbole
  - [quote: Merriam Webster definition of exaggeration]; hyperbole has same meaning
  - beyond fact/truth but not lies; common way of expressing strong feeling or opinion
  - second most used rhetorical device -> detection important for understanding human language/expression
- Text-only prior work vs. images
  - traditional studies: text modality, mainly single short sentences
  - but hyperbole not limited to text: "Winter comes early." - can't tell unless we see it is really that cold (Figure 1a)
  - images common on social media; can reveal hyperbole in text as facts (1a), express hyperbole themselves (1b), or together with text (1c)
  - some images only background, no help (1d) -> extra difficulty
- Weibo
  - one of the most popular social media in China and worldwide
  - many public posts with texts + images -> good resource for real-life multimodal hyperbole detection
  - just crawl enough posts automatically and annotate hyperbole / not
- Contributions
  - (1) first Chinese multimodal hyperbole detection dataset
  - (2) dataset analysis, statistical observations; how text + image together express hyperbole
  - (3) neural methods incl. unimodal and multimodal encoders; conclusions:
    - (3.1) image modality more useful than misleading; gating + attention -> fine performance; common sense = potential direction
    - (3.2) pre-trained multimodal methods perform badly vs. unimodal encoders + fusing; reason analyzed
    - (3.3) five disjoint keywords, disjoint contents; cross-domain performance poor; systematic bias between keywords is bottleneck for generalization, esp. for deep modality interaction

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Merriam Webster defines exaggeration as "an act or instance of exaggerating something: overstatement of the truth", and hyperbole means the same thing. Hyperbolic expressions say something that goes beyond the fact or the truth, but they are not seen as lies. Instead, hyperbole is a common way to express a strong feeling or opinion. Hyperbole is the second most used rhetorical device, so detecting it is very important for understanding human language and expression.

Traditional studies mostly focus on the text modality only. The datasets and methods they proposed mainly considered single short sentences. But hyperbole is not only expressed with text. For example, it is hard to know if the expression "Winter comes early." is hyperbolic or not unless we can see if it really is that cold (Figure 1a). Images are everywhere on social media and they play an important role in expressing exaggerated meanings. An image can be a fact that reveals the hyperbole in a text (Figure 1a), and it can also express hyperbole by itself (Figure 1b) or together with the text (Figure 1c). At the same time, some images are just background information and do not help to express hyperbole (Figure 1d), and this makes the task more difficult.

- Weibo
  - one of the most popular social media in China and all over the world
  - abundant public posts with texts + images -> perfect resource for real-life multimodal hyperbole detection
  - just crawl enough posts automatically, annotate hyperbole or not
- Contributions
  - (1) first Chinese multimodal hyperbole detection dataset, for further study
  - (2) dataset analysis + statistical observations; how text and image together express hyperbole
  - (3) neural methods (unimodal + multimodal encoders), conclusions:
    - (3.1) image more useful than misleading; gating + attention -> relatively fine performance; common sense as potential direction
    - (3.2) pre-trained multimodal methods do badly vs. unimodal encoders and fusing; reason analyzed
    - (3.3) five different, disjoint keywords; cross-domain results not good; systematic bias between keywords = bottleneck for generalization, esp. deep modality interaction

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Merriam Webster defines exaggeration as "an act or instance of exaggerating something: overstatement of the truth", and hyperbole means the same thing. Hyperbolic expressions say something that goes beyond the fact or the truth, but they are not seen as lies. Instead, hyperbole is a common way to express a strong feeling or opinion. Hyperbole is the second most used rhetorical device, so detecting it is very important for understanding human language and expression.

Traditional studies mostly focus on the text modality only. The datasets and methods they proposed mainly considered single short sentences. But hyperbole is not only expressed with text. For example, it is hard to know if the expression "Winter comes early." is hyperbolic or not unless we can see if it really is that cold (Figure 1a). Images are everywhere on social media and they play an important role in expressing exaggerated meanings. An image can be a fact that reveals the hyperbole in a text (Figure 1a), and it can also express hyperbole by itself (Figure 1b) or together with the text (Figure 1c). At the same time, some images are just background information and do not help to express hyperbole (Figure 1d), and this makes the task more difficult.

Weibo is one of the most popular social media in China and all over the world. It has a lot of publicly available posts with texts and images, so it is a perfect resource for real-life multimodal hyperbole detection. We only need to crawl enough posts from it automatically and annotate whether they are hyperbole or not.

Our contributions in this paper are the following: (1) We propose the first Chinese multimodal hyperbole detection dataset, which can be used for further study. (2) We analyze the dataset and get some statistical observations. We also summarize how the two modalities (text and image) express hyperbole together. (3) We use several neural methods for hyperbole detection, including unimodal and multimodal encoders, and we get these conclusions: (3.1) The image modality is more useful than misleading. With gating and attention mechanisms we can get relatively fine performance. We also point out that common sense is a potential direction for better results. (3.2) Pre-trained multimodal methods perform badly on this downstream task compared to unimodal encoders and fusing methods. We analyzed the reason. (3.3) The dataset is built on five different and disjoint keywords, with generally disjoint contents. When the methods are applied across domains they don't work very well. The systematic bias between posts with different keywords is the bottleneck that hinders generalization, especially for methods that need deep interactions between the modalities.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As defined by Merriam Webster, exaggeration means ‘‘an act or instance of exaggerating something: overstatement of the truth’’, and hyperbole has the same meaning. Though hyperbolic expressions state something beyond fact or truth, they are not considered lies. On the contrary, hyperbole is a common way of expressing one’s strong feeling or opinion. As hyperbole is the second most used rhetorical device [1], its detection is of great importance for understanding human language and expression.

Traditional studies focus mostly on the text modality. Their proposed datasets and methods mainly considered single short sentences ([2] [3], [4]). However, hyperbole is not expressed through text only. For example, we can hardly know whether the expression " Winter comes early. " is hyperbolic or not unless we can see whether it is indeed so cold (Figure 1a). Images, which are widely seen on social media, play an important role in expressing exaggerated meanings. They can serve as facts revealing the hyperbole contained in texts (Figure 1a), and they can also express hyperbole themselves (Figure 1b) or together with texts (Figure 1c). Meanwhile, some images just serve as background information and do not help the expression of hyperbole (Figure 1d), which adds further difficulty to this task.

Weibo is one of the most popular social media in China and all over the world. With its abundant publicly available posts with texts and images, it is a perfect resource for real-life multimodal hyperbole detection. We only need to automatically crawl enough posts from it and annotate them as hyperbole or not.

Our contributions in this paper can be summarized as follows: (1) We propose the first Chinese multimodal hyperbole detection dataset, which can be used for further study. (2) We analyze the dataset and obtain some statistical observations. We also summarize how the two modalities (text and image) together express hyperbole. (3) We employ several neural methods for hyperbole detection, including unimodal and multimodal encoders, and reach the following conclusions: (3.1) The image modality is more useful than misleading. With gating and attention mechanisms, we can achieve relatively fine performance. We also point out that common sense is a potential direction for achieving better results. (3.2) Compared with unimodal encoders and fusing methods, pre-trained multimodal methods perform badly on this downstream task. We analyzed the reason. (3.3) The dataset is built upon five different and disjoint keywords with generally disjoint contents. When applied across domains, the methods do not work very well. The systematic bias between posts with different keywords is the bottleneck hindering generalization ability, especially for methods requiring deep interactions between modalities.

References:
[1] Kreuz et al. (1996) Roger J. Kreuz, Richard M. Roberts, Brenda K. Johnson, and Eugenie L. Bertus. 1996. Figurative language occurrence and co-occurrence in contemporary literature. In Empirical Approaches to Literature and Aesthetics , pages 83–87, Norwood, NJ. Ablex Publishing Corporation.
[2] Troiano et al. (2018) Enrica Troiano, Carlo Strapparava, Gözde Özbal, and Serra Sinem Tekiroglu. 2018. A computational exploration of exaggeration. In Proceedings of the 2018 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing , page 3296–3304. Association for Computational Linguistics.
[3] Kong et al. (2020) Li Kong, Chuanyi Li, Jidong Ge, Bin Luo, and Vincent Ng. 2020. Identifying exaggerated language. In Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing , page 7024–7034. Association for Computational Linguistics.
[4] Biddle et al. (2021) Rhys Biddle, Maciek Rybinski, Qian Li, Cecile Paris, and Guandong Xu. 2021. Harnessing privileged information for hyperbole detection . In Proceedings of the The 19th Annual Workshop of the Australasian Language Technology Association , pages 58–67, Online. Australasian Language Technology Association.
